Chancellor John Healey Unveils £100 Energy Bill Support and Bank Tax Hike in First Budget

29 Oct 2026, 03:27 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Business Desk · Source: www.bbc.co.uk

Image: www.bbc.co.uk — Creative Commons

Key takeawaysChancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget to the House of Commons, introducing a series of measures aimed at easing cost-of-living pressures, including a one-off £100 energy payment funded by an increase in taxes on major banks. Addressing MPs in an hour-long sp

Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget to the House of Commons, introducing a series of measures aimed at easing cost-of-living pressures, including a one-off £100 energy payment funded by an increase in taxes on major banks.

Addressing MPs in an hour-long speech, Healey stated that the economic measures were designed to provide families with "breathing space now" against a backdrop of global economic challenges and rising oil prices stemming from conflict in the Middle East.

Key Financial and Cost of Living Measures

The central announcements in the Chancellor's package affect household energy, wages, and taxation:

  • Energy Support: Households in council tax bands A to D in England will receive a one-off £100 energy payment. Devolved administrations in Wales and Scotland indicated they intend to match or replicate the policy.
  • Standing Charges: Gas standing charges in England, Scotland, and Wales are scheduled to be scrapped during 2027 or as soon as possible thereafter, shifting fixed daily fees onto unit prices.
  • Fuel Duty: The temporary 5p cut on petrol and diesel fuel duty has been extended to July.
  • Minimum Wage: Minimum wage rates are set to increase by 3.9% in April.
  • Tax Adjustments: The tax on big bank profits will double from 3% to 6%, running from January next year to April 2028. Meanwhile, income tax thresholds remain frozen, and the cash ISA allowance will remain at £20,000 rather than being reduced.

For businesses, Healey increased the threshold at which high street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, though vape shops and adult gaming centres are excluded from this relief. The Chancellor also announced plans for regional mayors to retain 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to support local priorities.

Political Reaction and Economic Outlook

Opposition leaders criticized the measures as insufficient. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed," and criticized the absence of an immediate detailed plan to reach defense spending targets of 3% of national income by 2030.

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage similarly characterized the package as minor adjustments that fail to address broader structural issues, while representatives from the Institute for Fiscal Studies noted that the measures contain few elements likely to significantly accelerate economic growth.

Independent economic assessments from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded next year's growth forecast to 1%, projecting that British households will see limited financial improvement relative to pre-pandemic levels over the coming decade.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers seeking to understand how these measures directly impact personal finances, savings, and energy bills can review the official policy documents and parliamentary broadcasts.

  • Confirmed Facts: A £100 energy payment for bands A–D in England, a rise in bank profit taxes to 6%, an extension of the fuel duty cut, and a 3.9% minimum wage increase in April.
  • Unknowns and Future Decisions: Long-term defense spending implementation paths, final welfare reform legislation following ongoing reviews, and exact operational dates for the removal of gas standing charges in 2027.
